title: YInMn blue, the accidental blue of 2009
hook: Chemists hunting for electronics materials found a brand new blue instead.
peek: In 2009 a lab at Oregon State University heated a mix of oxides while looking for new electronic materials, and out came a vivid blue. YInMn blue was the first new inorganic blue pigment in about two centuries.
lede: In 2009, Mas Subramanian's lab at Oregon State University was looking for new materials for electronics. A graduate student, Andrew Smith, heated a mix of yttrium, indium and manganese oxides to over 1,000 degrees Celsius. The powder that came out of the furnace was a strikingly bright blue. It turned out to be the first new inorganic blue pigment found since cobalt blue in 1802.

bullets.text: The pigment is named after the chemical symbols of its ingredients: Y for yttrium, In for indium and Mn for manganese. Most people say it 'yin-min'.
Manganese often gives black or brown colours. In this particular crystal structure, the way the manganese atoms sit makes the material absorb red and green light and reflect a pure, intense blue.
YInMn blue also reflects a lot of infrared light, so surfaces painted with it stay cooler in the sun. That has made it interesting for roofs and coatings, not just for artists.
In 2017 Crayola released a crayon colour called Bluetiful, inspired by the discovery. The crayon does not contain the real pigment, which is still expensive, partly because indium is costly.
